speaker: Zoltan Pozsar
title: Zoltan Pozsar on His Next Big Move and the Coming Monetary Divorce
question: In global macro and rates markets, what happens to dollar funding plumbing when major commodity trades shift away from US dollar invoicing?
guest: Dollar shortages in certain regions are going to disappear when countries can source renminbi through PBOC swap lines. At the same time, regions that used to recycle dollar surpluses into the FX swap market—say, Australia putting dollars into the FX swap market for Japanese investors to hedge their Treasury portfolios—if they earn only half as many dollars because the other half is invoiced in renminbi, dollar recycling suffers. So the supply of and demand for dollars in FX swap markets gets redrawn, turning some positive cross-currency bases negative and some negative bases positive. On the rest of the world's demand for Treasuries, you historically needed dollars because essential imports were exclusively invoiced in dollars. China holds huge FX reserves as a life insurance policy because its annual import bill for major commodities like oil, gas, soybeans, and copper runs around five hundred billion dollars. If you can get commodity exporters to accept your own currency instead of dollars, you don't need to run with as many FX reserves, which pushes around marginal demand for Treasuries and dollar recycling across rates markets.

points.core: Commodity exporters invoicing outside dollars generate fewer surpluses to recycle into FX swaps.
points.note: Accept: reduced dollar export receipts shrinking the supply of dollars lent into FX swap markets by surplus countries. Do not credit: generic claims that de-dollarization reduces global dollar liquidity.

points.core: Altered regional dollar supply flips cross-currency swap bases across major funding corridors.
points.note: Accept: positive cross-currency bases turning negative or vice versa as regional dollar shortages disappear via alternative swap lines and surplus recycling shrinks. Do not credit: vague mentions of FX volatility.

points.core: Paying for commodity imports in domestic currency reduces precautionary Treasury reserve accumulation.
points.note: Accept: commodity importers needing smaller dollar FX reserve buffers (held largely in US Treasuries) as import insurance, lowering marginal foreign Treasury demand. Do not credit: generic statements that countries dislike holding US debt.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
When commodity trade moves away from dollar invoicing, the main effect is that fewer "petrodollars" get generated and recycled, which gradually thins a structural source of dollar liquidity outside the US.

Under dollar invoicing, exporters accumulate dollar receipts that are deposited in the eurodollar banking system, lent out through FX swaps, and invested in Treasuries by central banks and sovereign funds. If oil or other commodities are instead settled in yuan, rupees or dirhams, those surpluses stop flowing into offshore dollar deposits and reserve portfolios.

The likely consequences are a smaller price-insensitive foreign bid for Treasuries, which adds upward pressure on term premia, and a greater reliance on private, price-sensitive buyers financed through repo. Offshore dollar deposit funding for non-US banks also shrinks.

Dollar debt, however, does not shrink in step. Borrowers with dollar liabilities but fewer natural dollar revenues must source dollars synthetically, which can widen cross-currency basis spreads and make funding more fragile in stress, increasing dependence on Fed swap lines and the FIMA repo facility.

In practice the shift has been marginal so far, because dollar dominance in funding, collateral and hedging markets is far stickier than in invoicing.

points.why: The response identifies exporters’ dollar receipts as a source of FX swap lending and says non-dollar settlement shrinks those receipts.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: When major commodity trades shift away from US dollar invoicing, offshore dollar supply and trade-finance demand both contract, rewiring money-market plumbing asymmetrically. Historically, dollar commodity surpluses generated large offshore balances that exporters recycled into US Treasury bills, Eurodollar deposits, the Fed’s foreign repo pool, and FX swaps. Settling trades in other currencies shrinks this price-insensitive liquidity pool, softening captive foreign demand for front-end Treasuries and nudging bill yields and repo rates marginally higher relative to OIS. Meanwhile, importers and trading houses need less short-term dollar trade credit. Crucially, however, global debt, commodity derivatives benchmarks, and margin calls remain overwhelmingly dollar-denominated. Losing dollar export receipts strips producers and emerging-market borrowers of natural cash-flow hedges while draining the offshore deposits banks use to fund them, and exporters paid in less-liquid currencies often swap proceeds back into dollars anyway. Participants must therefore lean harder on dealer-intermediated FX swaps and bilateral central-bank swap lines, fragmenting liquidity and leaving cross-currency basis spreads more prone to acute dollar squeezes during stress.

points.why: The response explicitly links non-dollar settlement to a smaller pool of exporter dollar receipts available for recycling into FX swaps.

noweb.answer: When major commodity trades shift away from US dollar invoicing, the offshore Eurodollar loop contracts asymmetrically, reshaping global funding plumbing. Historically, dollar invoicing required importers to borrow short-term dollars for trade finance while exporters recycled revenue surpluses into Eurodollar deposits, commercial paper, FX swaps, and US Treasuries. Switching to non-dollar invoicing curbs transactional demand for dollar trade credit, yet global financial balance sheets remain heavily dollarized, and thin local cross-rates often still route currency hedging through dollar FX swaps as the vehicle currency. Meanwhile, exporters accumulate non-dollar balances instead of sticky offshore dollar deposits, draining a stable, low-cost funding pool from international banks and money markets. Non-US institutions carrying legacy dollar assets must replace those lost deposits via wholesale markets and FX swaps, leaving cross-currency basis spreads more prone to widening and increasing reliance on Federal Reserve swap lines during stress. Simultaneously, weaker surplus recycling into bills and Treasuries forces domestic dealers and money market funds to absorb more sovereign supply, crowding dealer balance sheets, lifting term premia, and tightening onshore repo rates and SOFR spreads.

points.why: The response identifies FX swaps as a historical outlet for exporter surpluses, but its account of lost exporter funding specifies offshore deposits and leaves the effect on dollar supply in FX swaps unstated.
The response predicts wider cross-currency basis spreads without describing sign reversals across regional funding corridors.
The response attributes weaker foreign Treasury demand to reduced exporter recycling and omits the decline in importers’ need for precautionary dollar reserves.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly, very little changes at first, and what does change happens slowly. Dollar invoicing of commodities creates some of the offshore demand for dollars. Traders and non-US banks need dollar trade finance, Eurodollar deposits and FX-swap funding, and exporters' surplus dollars get "recycled" into Treasuries, repo and US bank deposits. If oil, LNG or metals are invoiced in yuan, euros or local currencies, that flow-driven demand shrinks a little. Over time that could ease pressure on the cross-currency basis, reduce reliance on Fed swap lines during stress, and cut foreign official buying of Treasuries. Less official buying could raise term premia slightly.

The catch is that invoicing is only a small part of why the world needs dollars. The bigger driver is the roughly $13 trillion of dollar debt owed outside the US (BIS estimate), along with derivatives, collateral and hedging. That stock still has to be rolled over and hedged in dollars. Commodity traders also often borrow in dollars even when they invoice in other currencies.

The more likely result is fragmentation. Parallel networks grow, such as China's CIPS payment system, PBoC currency swap lines and offshore yuan liquidity pools. That adds basis risk and operational complexity during the transition, but it doesn't replace the dollar funding system.

points.why: The response describes exporters recycling dollars into Treasuries, repo, and bank deposits but never explains how lower dollar export receipts reduce the supply of dollars lent through FX swaps.
The response mentions easing basis pressure and PBoC swap lines but does not explain how changes in regional dollar supply and demand can reverse the sign of cross-currency bases.
The response predicts reduced official Treasury buying without linking it to commodity importers needing smaller precautionary dollar reserve buffers when they can pay in their own currencies.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
When major commodity trades shift away from US dollar invoicing, the core effect on dollar funding plumbing is a shrinkage of the offshore recycling loop that supplies cheap dollar liquidity. Under dollar invoicing, commodity exporters accumulate dollar surpluses and recycle them into Eurodollar bank deposits, commercial paper, repo markets, and US Treasuries. Settling in other currencies reduces this organic offshore inflow, curbing a steady source of wholesale dollar funding for foreign banks and marginal demand for Treasuries.

Because global debt, trade credit, and hedging remain overwhelmingly dollar-denominated, demand for dollars falls far less than this supply. Foreign banks and borrowers must therefore rely more heavily on FX swaps and US dealer balance sheets to obtain dollars, widening cross-currency basis spreads and raising offshore funding costs, especially during market stress. At the margin, reduced automatic recycling into Treasuries can lift US term premia and make global dollar liquidity more reliant on domestic US reserves and Federal Reserve swap lines.

points.why: The response links lower exporter dollar receipts to less wholesale funding and greater reliance on FX swaps, but never says exporters supply fewer dollars to the FX swap market.
The response predicts wider cross-currency basis spreads and higher offshore funding costs without describing sign reversals as regional dollar supply and demand shift.
The response attributes weaker Treasury demand to reduced exporter recycling and omits how paying in domestic currency reduces importers’ need for precautionary dollar reserves.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
If commodity trades shift both invoicing and settlement away from the dollar, importers need fewer dollars to pay suppliers, and banks may see less demand for dollar trade credit and FX swaps that raise dollars. Dollar clearing volumes can fall, while financing and hedging demand grows in the currencies used for settlement.

Commodity exporters also receive fewer dollars directly to place in bank deposits or invest in Treasuries. They may still convert the proceeds into dollars, so the effect on dollar funding costs depends on both sides. If demand for dollar funding falls faster than supply, the premium for borrowing dollars through FX swaps tends to shrink. If dollar funding supply falls faster, the premium can rise.

The shift affects trade-related flows first. Existing dollar debts still need servicing, and dollar-priced benchmarks and dollar collateral can sustain hedging and liquidity needs even when the invoice currency changes.

points.why: The response links lower exporter dollar receipts to deposits and Treasury purchases but never states that exporters supply fewer dollars to FX swap markets.
The response discusses borrowing premiums rising or falling without identifying cross-currency bases changing sign across regional funding corridors.
The response notes that importers need fewer dollars for payments but does not connect this to smaller precautionary reserves and lower marginal Treasury demand.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
When a commodity trade shifts out of dollars, the importer needs less short-term dollar funding to pay the invoice, and the exporter receives fewer dollars to hold in deposits or reinvest in Treasuries. Some payments and working-capital finance move into the new currency.

The net effect depends on what happens after settlement. If the exporter swaps the proceeds into dollars to service dollar debt or buy dollar assets, dollar demand shifts into the FX swap market. If both sides also move their borrowing, hedging and cash balances into the new currency, demand for dollar funding falls more durably.

For rates markets, the distinction matters. Fewer dollar invoices alone tell you little about Treasury yields or the cross-currency basis, the premium or discount on obtaining dollars through FX swaps. Those depend on where exporters invest their receipts, who still needs to borrow dollars, and how readily banks can supply them.

points.why: The response links fewer dollar export receipts to deposits and Treasury purchases but never connects them to a reduction in dollars supplied to FX swaps.
The response defines the cross-currency basis and lists its determinants without stating that regional funding shifts can reverse its sign.
The response identifies lower short-term dollar funding needs for importers but never links them to smaller precautionary reserves or lower marginal Treasury demand.
